title: Can we spot buttons that look usable but have no accessible name?
question: Could comparing what a button looks like with what a screen reader receives help us find missed accessibility problems?
answer: ASE—Auditable Symbiotic Ecosystem—is human-guided AI software development through voluntary contribution and shared learning. Its relay's 2026-10-19 research digest describes an outside idea: add computer vision to rules-based accessibility checks to spot interactive elements that markup does not describe (F18, MEDIUM confidence; we have not independently verified the web research). We propose an ASE rehearsal that compares synthetic screenshots with accessibility trees—the names, roles and states exposed to assistive technology—for task details, Artifacts controls or read-only Mission Control. To test its added value, we would compare rules-only with rules-plus-AI findings across 12 synthetic pairs—six seeded discrepancies and six matched controls—and require detection of at least five seeded discrepancies, at most one false positive, and links from every finding to its screenshot region and tree node. These checks have not run; passing would justify further review, not prove accessibility conformance or human acceptance.

art.title: Visible button, missing name
art.statement: A synthetic screenshot shows a Download button beside an accessibility-tree node with an empty name. Words and a comparison mark identify the mismatch without relying on color.
